Supplement to the poster · Winter Simulation Conference 2026

Bayesian Optimization in High-Dimensional, Mixed Search Spaces Using Block-Partitioned Tree-Structured Parzen Estimators

Vipul Chalotra, Sasan Amini, and Inneke Van Nieuwenhuyse

Computational Mathematics Research Group, Data Science Institute, and FlandersMake@UHasselt, Hasselt University, Belgium · vipul.chalotra@uhasselt.be

This page follows the poster panel by panel. Each panel repeats the poster's text, then shows the poster's figure next to the full table behind it, with the settings and protocol. An evaluation is one call of the objective (for example, one simulation); a replication is one complete optimization with its own random seed.

Tap or click a figure to enlarge it.

AbstractKey findings1Why TPE2Block-TPE 3Random blocks4Scaling5Kriging-based BO References

Abstract

Simulation optimization often requires optimizing expensive black-box functions over high-dimensional, mixed decision spaces under tight evaluation budgets. The well-established kriging-based Bayesian optimization (BO) does not naturally accommodate such search spaces: the common covariance kernels are only defined for continuous inputs, and the computational cost scales cubically with the sample size. In contrast, Tree-structured Parzen Estimators (TPE) handle mixed and conditional search spaces natively and scale linearly. Their drawbacks are that kernel density estimates degrade as dimension grows, and that current frameworks assume deterministic objectives. In this work, we address the first: block-partitioned TPE (Block-TPE) splits the decision variables into small blocks and performs density estimation within each low-dimensional subspace. Comparing random, correlation-informed, and oracle partitions on synthetic, continuous, and categorical testbeds up to 160 dimensions, we find that partition quality matters far less than partitioning itself: Block-TPE outperforms or stays competitive with state-of-the-art high-dimensional, mixed-variable BO algorithms at fractional cost.

The abstract and the poster name the partition strategies differently:

  • random partition redrawn periodically = random blocks re-drawn every 10 evaluations
  • random partition held fixed = random blocks fixed for all evaluations
  • correlation-informed partition = blocks learned from correlations
  • oracle partition = fixed blocks of truly interacting variables

KEY FINDINGS

  • Frequently re-drawing random blocks beats learning blocks from correlations: no structure learning needed (see 3).
  • The gain over Optuna's TPE models grows with the number of variables, for both continuous and mixed-variable problems (see 4).
  • Close to the best kriging-based methods, in seconds instead of minutes to hours (see 5).
1

Why TPE and not kriging?

Simulation optimization often has many decision variables (continuous, integer, categorical), and only a small budget. Kriging-based Bayesian optimization struggles in mixed-variable search spaces and settings with many variables.

The Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) handles every variable type natively: it splits past evaluations into good and bad and places the next evaluation where good evaluations are dense and bad ones sparse. But its density models weaken as the number of variables grows.

TPE as used throughout (Optuna's defaults).
Good evaluationsthe best 10% of the \(n\) evaluations so far, at most 25: \(\min(\lceil 0.1\,n\rceil, 25)\)
Bad evaluationsthe rest
Density of good evaluations\(l(x)\): a Parzen estimator, a weighted sum of kernels centred on the good evaluations
Density of bad evaluations\(g(x)\): the same, on the bad evaluations
Next evaluationdraw 24 candidates from \(l(x)\); evaluate the one with the largest \(l(x)/g(x)\)
Continuous and integer variables1-D Gaussian kernels, truncated to the variable's bounds
Categorical variablesa kernel over the categories; no order between categories is assumed
ImplementationOptuna's TPESampler, default settings (Akiba et al. 2019)
2

Block-TPE: small random blocks of variables

Block-TPE splits the variables at random into small blocks, fits one multivariate density model per block, and merges their proposed decision values for evaluation. The blocks remain unchanged for a few evaluations, before they are randomly re-drawn again.

Why it helps: Block-TPE provides a better balance between exploitation and exploration than the univariate and multivariate TPE models, particularly in high dimensions.

Univariate TPE

\[p(x)=\prod_{d=1}^{D}\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\,p_{k,d}(x_d)\]

Block-TPE

\[p(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\prod_{d=1}^{b_i}p_{k,d}(x_d)\]

Multivariate TPE

\[p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\prod_{d=1}^{D}p_{k,d}(x_d)\]
\(K\) =number of components\(B\) =total number of blocks \(D\) =total number of variables\(b_i\) =number of variables in block \(i\) \(w_k\) =weight of component \(k\)\(p_{k,d}(x)\) =1-D kernel of component \(k\) on variable \(d\) \(x_d\) =input data of variable \(d\)\(p(x)\) =density \(l(x)\) of the good evaluations, or \(g(x)\) of the rest
  1. Split. Shuffle the \(D\) variables and cut them into consecutive blocks whose sizes are drawn uniformly from 1 to 10; the last block takes the variables that are left.
  2. Model each block. Fit \(l\) and \(g\) jointly over the block's variables only, from the same split of all evaluations into good and bad; draw 24 candidates and keep the one with the largest \(l/g\).
  3. Merge. The blocks' winning values together form the next evaluation.
  4. Re-draw. Draw new random blocks every 10 completed evaluations.
Block-TPE settings in every experiment on this page.
Largest block size10
Block sizesuniform from 1 to 10; the last block takes the rest
Blocks re-drawnevery 10 completed evaluations
Good evaluationsbest 10%, at most 25 (Optuna's default)
Candidates per block24
Kernels and bandwidthsOptuna's defaults; a block can mix continuous, integer and categorical variables
Initial design\(D\) evaluations; blocking starts after it
Implementationan Optuna sampler built on TPESampler
3

Is blocking randomly the right choice?

Block-TPE (random blocks re-drawn every 10 evaluations) beats Block-TPE (fixed blocks of truly interacting variables). Blocks learned from correlations do no better than chance.

Block-learning mechanisms add computational costs without improving the performance.

Problems

Each problem is a sum of independent blocks of 10 variables: strong interactions inside each block, none between blocks, so the truly interacting variables are known.

  • Rotated ellipsoid, Rosenbrock and mix (blocks cycling ellipsoid, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin): continuous variables in [−5, 5], each block randomly rotated and shifted.
  • Mixed ellipsoid and Rosenbrock: each block has 6 continuous variables and 4 categorical variables with 5 categories; every category maps to a fixed random value, and the block's 10 values go through one rotated function.

Every replication draws a new instance: new rotations, shifts, and positions of the blocks among the variables.

Strategies

Budget: 10 evaluations per variable. The first D evaluations are random and shared by all strategies within a replication; 10 replications per problem and number of variables. All Block-TPE strategies use blocks of 1 to 10 variables.

  • random, re-drawn every 10 evaluations: Block-TPE as in panel 2;
  • learned from correlations every 10 evaluations: blocks of the same random sizes, filled greedily with the most correlated variables (Spearman rank correlation over the best quarter of evaluations; categories coded by their mean objective rank);
  • random, fixed for all evaluations: random blocks drawn once;
  • fixed blocks of truly interacting variables: the reference;
  • Optuna's multivariate and univariate TPE.

Measure

Each number is the share of paired replications (same problem, number of variables and seed) in which a strategy's best value beats the reference's; ties count half, so 50% means as good as the reference. The 95% intervals resample whole problems (2,000 bootstrap draws).

At 160 variables the fixed true blocks win every replication on the two ellipsoid problems, whose blocks are strongly coupled and ill-conditioned.

Blocks learned from correlations

For every re-draw of the learned blocks, the precision is the share of variable pairs placed in one block that truly interact; the table averages it over all re-draws and replications. Chance is the share of all variable pairs that truly interact, which is what pairing variables at random gives. The ratio of the two lies between 0.97 and 1.04 for every problem and number of variables: the correlations recover no more structure than chance.

Head to head, Block-TPE matches the learned blocks at 40 variables and beats them at 80 and 160 variables (table on the right, top).

4

Does it scale?

24 continuous and 24 mixed-integer COCO functions, and 12 mixed-variable functions with 5 to 20 categories per categorical variable, for 10–160 dimensions. Evaluation budget: 10 · d

For d ≥ 20, Block-TPE beats Optuna's multivariate TPE (best TPE model) on 20 to 23 of 24 functions in both COCO suites and on 11 of 12 mixed-variable ones (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05). Block-TPE (EI), which weights good evaluations by their quality, lowers the error further.

Test suites

Each at 10, 20, 40, 80 and 160 variables.

  • Continuous: the 24 BBOB functions of COCO (Hansen et al. 2021), box [−5, 5].
  • Mixed-integer: the 24 functions of COCO's bbob-mixint suite (Tušar et al. 2019).
  • Mixed-variable: 12 functions whose variables cycle categorical, integer, continuous; categorical variables have 5, 10, 15 or 20 categories (instances 1–4), placed equally far apart so that no category lies between two others; integer variables have 11 levels; the optimum is a random decision with known value.

Protocol

Budget: 10 evaluations per variable. The first D evaluations form a design shared by all methods (a Latin hypercube on continuous variables, uniform levels and categories otherwise). Replications: 4 instances × 5 seeds per function and number of variables in the two COCO suites, 4 instances × 10 seeds in the mixed-variable suite; 36,000 replications over all methods. Methods: random search, Optuna's univariate and multivariate TPE, Block-TPE and Block-TPE (EI).

Measure

Error = best value found − optimal value, floored at 10−8. “% of random search's” is the geometric mean, over replications, of a method's error divided by random search's error on the same instance and seed. A function is won when the method's geometric-mean error on it is lower; the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compares the two methods' per-function means of log error.

Block-TPE (EI)

The same blocks, with one change to the density of good evaluations: each good evaluation is weighted by its improvement over the worst good value, \(w_i \propto y_{\mathrm{thr}} - y_i\) (minimization), rescaled to mean 1; the bad evaluations keep equal weights. TPE's ratio \(l/g\) corresponds to the probability of improvement; weighting the good evaluations by improvement turns it into an expected-improvement criterion (Song et al. 2022).

Comparison with kriging-based BO methods

21, mostly high-dimensional kriging-based BO, methods for continuous problems. Block-TPE (EI), median rank 5 in 14 s, is behind only HEBO, TuRBO-1 & Vanilla BO (Hvarfner), at 191–1,830 s.

20 continuous plus 20 categorical variables, against leading mixed-variable methods: Block-TPE (EI) is best on RosenbrockCLO and second on the other two, behind Bounce (400x slower).

Setup

The BBOB comparison of Santoni et al. (2024): 24 functions, 3 instances, 40 variables, an initial design of 40 evaluations and a budget of 10 evaluations per variable plus 50 (450 evaluations). Sources:

  • published: the 12 methods of that comparison, from its deposited data (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.11215990); missing SAASBO and HEBO cells were filled in with the authors' code where feasible;
  • added: five further high-dimensional methods under the same protocol: BAxUS (Papenmeier et al. 2022), REMBO (Wang et al. 2016), HeSBO (Nayebi et al. 2019), ALEBO (Letham et al. 2020) and vanilla BO with a dimension-scaled lengthscale prior (Hvarfner et al. 2024);
  • TPE: the four TPE methods.

Ranks

In each function–instance cell, methods are ranked by their mean final distance to the optimum over the cell's replications, among the methods present in that cell. The table gives the median and quartiles of a method's ranks over the 72 cells (fewer where replications are missing).

Time

Median wall-clock time per replication, every method on one CPU core with one thread, on the same cluster partition (VSC wICE). Replications were stopped after one hour; “≥3,600” marks methods for which at least half the timed replications hit that cap, so the median is a lower bound.

Problems

The three mixed-category problems of the CatCMA benchmark (Hamano et al. 2024), each with 20 continuous variables in [−3, 3] and 20 categorical variables with 10 categories: SphereCOM (sphere plus categorical OneMax), RosenbrockCLO (Rosenbrock plus categorical LeadingOnes) and MCProximity (each continuous variable must track a target set by its category). The optimum is moved to a random point in every replication, as in the benchmark of Bounce (Papenmeier et al. 2023), so no method can exploit an optimum at the centre or at the first category.

Protocol

400 evaluations, a shared initial design of 40, 10 replications per problem. Methods: Bounce, CoCaBO (Ru et al. 2020), Casmopolitan (Wan et al. 2021) and BODi (Deshwal et al. 2023), the last three through the MCBO framework (Dreczkowski et al. 2023), plus CatCMA and Optuna's two TPE models.

Time

The four kriging-based methods used 4 cores and 4 threads per replication; Block-TPE and Block-TPE (EI) were re-timed on 1 core and 1 thread on the same partition (Intel Xeon Platinum 8360Y), and the re-timed replications reproduce the plotted results exactly. Block-TPE (EI) takes a median 10.2 s; the kriging-based methods take 204 to 397 times longer while using four cores (Bounce 397 times, over the 28 replications with stored times). Optuna's TPE models and CatCMA were not re-timed.
